title: Millions in City Contracts Went to Companies the U.S. Says Are Tied to the Cartel del Noreste — Nuevo Laredo Admits It
excerpt: The U.S. Treasury sanctioned 11 companies for alleged Cartel del Noreste ties — and Nuevo Laredo's city government admitted two of them held city contracts worth 22.3 million pesos.
content:
Less than a week after the United States Treasury Department named 11 companies it says are tied to the Cartel del Noreste, the city government of Nuevo Laredo has admitted the uncomfortable part: two of those companies were in its own vendor rolls — and one of them collected millions of pesos in city contracts.

What the U.S. announced

On October 13, 2026, the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) sanctioned four individuals and 11 entities it alleges are connected to the Cartel del Noreste (CDN), the organization formerly known as Los Zetas. The U.S. State Department designated the CDN a Foreign Terrorist Organization in February 2025, and Treasury called this its largest action yet against the cartel's finances.

Among the sanctioned firms are two Nuevo Laredo construction companies: Construcciones y Edificaciones Garza Elías (CEGESA) and Concretos y Productos Asfálticos del Norte (COPASA). According to the U.S. investigation, both were "among the few construction companies authorized by the Northeast Cartel to carry out construction work in Nuevo Laredo, Tamaulipas" — in other words, the cartel allegedly decided who got to pour concrete in the city.

What City Hall admitted

After the sanctions were announced, the municipal government of Nuevo Laredo acknowledged that both companies appear in its registries of suppliers and contractors and have held contractual relationships with the city. The city says it has ordered an audit of the procedures and public resources tied to the two firms.

Records reviewed by LatinUS on Mexico's National Transparency Platform show the scale of the COPASA relationship: the city awarded the company six contracts between 2024 and 2026 totaling 22.3 million pesos, all during the administration of Mayor Carmen Lilia Canturosas Villarreal. Three contracts in 2026 alone totaled 9.4 million pesos for asphalt resurfacing on city streets; three more in 2025 added up to 12.9 million pesos.

COPASA was founded by Gamaliel Garza García, one of the four individuals named in the U.S. sanctions. U.S. authorities also link him to a horse-racing and betting operation on the outskirts of Nuevo Laredo that Treasury says laundered cartel proceeds.

The state says: not us

The Tamaulipas state government, led by Governor Américo Villarreal Anaya, drew a sharp line. After reviewing its public-works contractor and supplier registries, the state says none of the sanctioned individuals or companies has held a state contract since October 1, 2022 — and the state's anti-corruption office has instructed every agency to block any registration, award, or contract involving the designated persons or firms.

What to watch

These are U.S. allegations. No court has tested them, and everyone named is presumed innocent unless proven otherwise. The open questions now sit with City Hall: what did the city's vetting process miss, what will the audit find, and will any officials face consequences for contracts signed with firms the U.S. says answered to the cartel?
